BLOCK TEMPLATES Templates are Gutenberg frames stored in WordPress. They use blocks installed by the active theme and plugins. These tools create no block types, PHP files or scripts. Existing theme PHP files may be selected as Content Source rules; the file is provided and maintained by the theme developer. List templates before creating, then get-template before editing. Fabrement > Templates opens the template list directly; open a template to add, move and edit installed blocks in Gutenberg.
save-template requires mode create, replace or edit. Create needs title and blocks. Replace sends the complete frame, or omits blocks to rename/change metadata only. Edit uses edits and expectedHash from get-template; an outdated hash refuses the write. Preserve unrelated and unknown saved markup. Use exactly one content slot for the page's own content; it may be nested in a group: {name:"fabrement/content-source"}, or core/post-content (which cannot select theme PHP files). Slot attributes survive edits. All other blocks follow block-discovery-contract and content-contract: a dynamic PHP renderer alone does not establish save() semantics. ACF data is validated against existing field definitions. Unsafe new or changed HTML/attributes are refused atomically.
THEME PHP SOURCES list-theme-templates returns available files under templates/ in the active and parent themes. It returns paths and declared view kinds, not source code. Child files shadow parent files at the same relative path. Never invent paths, upload PHP or use other tools to bypass a missing file. save-template accepts contentSource:{rules:[{context:"singular:page",file:"body.php"}]}. Omit contentSource to preserve it; rules:[] restores page content. Rules are stored in one shared JSON manifest for the template and all translations, and returned separately by get-template. The slot reads them from that manifest each time the template is drawn: never send rules or templateId in block attributes; such a block is refused. Nonempty rules require fabrement/content-source; native core/post-content does not select PHP files. The block's Gutenberg sidebar offers the same choices. Contexts: singular:<type>, archive:<type>, blog-home, 404, tax, tax:<taxonomy>, tax:<taxonomy>:<termId>. A file may declare Fabrement: singular/archive or an exact context; respect its declared kind. The renderer rechecks paths and excludes traversal, external paths and escaped symlinks. If the file disappears or throws, the slot falls back to the page's own content (the posts page's on the blog index) without modifying it. Theme code runs as theme code; the content HTML checks do not audit the developer's PHP implementation.
HEADERS AND FOOTERS Create reusable headers/footers with save-synced-pattern and kind header/footer, filled with existing core, ACF or registered blocks. Place them in the frame as {name:"core/block",attributes:{ref:123}}. One shared header edit updates all templates using it. Ordinary blocks can also sit directly in the frame. Use theme/plugin styling or supported Gutenberg design controls.
ASSIGNMENT assign-template-pages with mode add affects only the supplied pageIds. Remove releases those pages. Replace makes pageIds the entire assigned set: use only after inspecting list-template-pages. set-default-template sets a default for a public post type; explicit page template picks take priority. Classic themes with front-page.php and block themes with front-page may override a type default on the homepage. Preview the actual assigned page, not just the saved frame. assign-template-archive binds archive contexts; build the listing with installed Query blocks or an existing theme PHP source authored for archive views. core/post-content within an archive Query's Post Template renders each result's content. delete-template refuses in-use templates unless force is explicit; deletion clears assignments, defaults and archive bindings. It does not delete page content or shared header/footer patterns.
Native editor drafts are not assignable until published. The MCP save-template publishes the template because it is a shared layout, not a page. Verify an assigned page's frontend and Gutenberg editor. For multilingual templates, read template-translation; never create duplicate originals to translate.
